Learning Objectives
Specify the epidemiology, etiology, and risk factors for olecranon fractures.
Perform an appropriate workup and assessment for patients in whom elbow trauma is
suspected.
Discuss the surgical and nonsurgical management of olecranon fractures.
Specify the differences between simple and complex olecranon fracture patterns and identify
which patterns may involve additional elbow instability.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Olecranon fractures occur frequently, representing approximately 10% of fractures to the
upper extremity.1

The subcutaneous nature of the bone limits soft-tissue and muscular coverage; therefore, a
direct blow or fall may lead to fracture.
Olecranon fractures are categorized as simple or complex based on fracture pattern and
overall elbow stability.
Management includes nonsurgical and surgical treatment modalities.
Identification of olecranon fractures with associated elbow instability is critical to successful
management.
Epidemiology
Olecranon fractures represent approximately 1% of fractures in adults and 20% of proximal
forearm fractures, with an incidence of approximately 11.5 to 12 per 100,000 per year.1-3
Olecranon fractures affect patients of all ages, and incidence increases with age.
The incidence of olecranon fractures in the elderly is rising with increased longevity and
improved medical care.4
Displaced olecranon fractures are most common; however, a small proportion (10% to 12%)
are nondisplaced and stable (approximately 12%).5-7

Epidemiology
Two observational studies from Edinburgh, Scotland, review the epidemiology of
olecranon fractures. Duckworth et al1 and Court-Brown and Caesar3 reported that
fractures of the olecranon are common in all age groups and are increasingly common in
the elderly population, particular individuals in their late fifties. Most fractures through
the olecranon represent displaced injury patterns likely driven by anatomic and
biomechanical reasons. The pull of the triceps and the fulcrum lever of the trochlear
notch inherently introduce deforming forces. In addition, elbow instability results from
disruption of olecranon and proximal ulnar anatomy, and complex injury patterns
present treatment challenges if not adequately managed. Although simple transverse
fracture patterns are most common, special attention should be paid to injuries
extending into the surrounding ligamentous and bony structures to avoid missing more
complex injuries, such as Monteggia and transolecranon fracture-dislocations.8

Regardless of the injury pattern and fracture morphology, management focuses on
restoration of the greater sigmoid notch articulation and triceps attachment.7
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The proximal ulna consists of two articular surfaces: the greater and lesser sigmoid notches.
Through these surfaces the proximal ulna is intimately congruent with the radial head and the
distal humerus.
The greater sigmoid notch extends from the olecranon tip to the coronoid and articulates with
the trochlea.
The olecranon forms a bony stabilizer against anterior dislocation, whereas the coronoid
process provides resistance to posterior instability.
Ligamentous structures (medial and lateral collateral ligamentous complexes) have defined
bony landmarks and attachments (sublime tubercle and crista supinatoris) that confer
ligamentous stability to the elbow.
Predictable, reproducible reconstruction of anatomic alignment of the proximal olecranon
requires an understanding of proximal ulnar dorsal angulation (PUDA), varus angulation, and
olecranon-diaphysis angles.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Despite a rather straightforward radiographic appearance, proximal anatomy of the ulna
is complex. The osseous stability of the elbow is framed by the ulnohumeral and
radioulnar joints. The ulnohumeral joint, a basic hinge joint formed by the trochlea and
the greater sigmoid notch, provides inherent stability to the elbow. The proximal
radioulnar joint, formed by the radial head and the lesser sigmoid notch, allows for
forearm rotation. The olecranon, the proximal segment of the greater sigmoid notch, is
separated from the coronoid, the anterior border of the greater sigmoid notch, by the
trochlear groove. In addition, a bare area of 3 to 5 mm is present within the articular
surface of the trochlear groove.9,10 Several recently defined proximal ulna anatomic
variables have been described in the literature. The greater sigmoid notch (trochlear
groove) is angled approximately 27o posteriorly, matching the anterior angulation of the

distal humerus (radiographic olecranon-diaphysis angle or articular angle)11 (Resource
1). As described by Rouleau et al12 the PUDA is critical for radioulnar stability and is
reported to be approximately 5.7o maximal at 4.7 cm distal to the olecranon tip.13 The
proximal ulna also bows in the coronal plane, generating a varus alignment angle of
approximately 17.5o, with a wide variation of 9.3o to 23o).11,14,15 These values appear to
be patient- and gender-specific with considerable variation, indicating the need for
thoughtful evaluation and contralateral side measurement before reconstruction.16-18
Beyond the bony anatomy of the proximal ulna, ligamentous stability is critical for
stabilization of the elbow and the ulnohumeral joint. Studies have described the
important roles of the medial and lateral collateral ligaments and the role of the dynamic
stabilizers of the elbow.19-23 An understanding of the proximal ulna attachment points
for these structures is important to avoid missing a potential injury to these important
stabilizers. The ligamentous insertions from the medial and lateral side are intricately
connected to the proximal ulna and olecranon. The medial collateral ligament inserts 2.8
mm from the ulnar articular surface onto the sublime tubercle, whereas the lateral
collateral ligament complex inserts laterally onto the crista supinatoris.24,25 Careful
scrutiny of these areas after elbow trauma may help identify the potential for soft-tissue
instability or combined bony and ligamentous trauma.
The triceps tendon inserts onto the olecranon and expands onto the proximal ulna as it
incorporates into the periosteum.26 This insertion is localized onto the dorsal surface
rather than the tip of the olecranon; therefore, in olecranon fractures, the extensor
mechanism may be disrupted, leading to with the potential for a decrease or loss in
active elbow extension.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Olecranon fractures occur via direct and indirect mechanisms of injury and are dictated by the
mechanics and energy imparted during trauma.27


Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Olecranon fractures may result from high-energy trauma and low-energy falls.1,3,28-30
Approximately 70% of fractures occur via a low-energy mechanism.4,5 Ipsilateral injuries
reportedly occur in approximately 20% of patients.1 The direct mechanism of injury
typically occurs as force is directed at the point of the elbow, thereby driving the distal
humerus (trochlea) onto the greater sigmoid notch. Depending on elbow position and
force, simple or comminuted fracture patterns may result. Alternatively, a second
mechanism for fracture occurs with a forceful contraction of the triceps with the elbow
in a semi-flexed position while breaking a fall. This may result in an avulsion-type
fracture through the olecranon, resulting in an indirect mechanism of injury.31 Lower-
demand osteoporotic elderly patients are more commonly at risk of this type of injury
pattern (Resource 2).
Risk Factors
Olecranon fractures follow a type F distribution curve.
Most commonly, olecranon fractures in elderly patients are sustained after low-energy trauma.
Most of these injuries are simple displaced fractures.1
In contrast, fractures in young patients typically are caused by high-energy mechanisms of
injury.
Osteopenia, osteoporosis, and an increasing fall risk are major risk factors for low-energy
fractures in elderly patients.

Risk Factors
Olecranon fractures follow a type F fracture distribution curve. Therefore, advanced age
is associated with a corresponding increased risk of fracture. Although patients are
defined as elderly by their chronologic age, physiologic and functional markers of patient
status may be better indicators of overall health.32,33 Elderly patients, particularly those
with osteoporosis, are at risk for an olecranon fracture after a low-energy. traumatic

mechanism of injury, such as a fall from standing height. Olecranon fractures, similar to
other fragility fractures, may be a sentinel event indicating the need for preventative
management to reduce associated fragility fracture risk.1
Associated Injuries
Open fractures are surprisingly rare despite the subcutaneous location of the ulna.1,3,4
Ulnar neuropathy or irritation is uncommon.
Concomitant ipsilateral limb injuries occur in as many as 25% of patients with a proximal ulna
fracture.
For transolecranon and Monteggia fracture-dislocation variants, patterns are important to
identify and appropriately manage.
A high index of suspicion should be maintained to identify potential associated bony and soft-
tissue trauma.

Associated Injuries
Ulnar nerve injury and symptoms are uncommon after olecranon fracture despite the
proximity of the nerve medially. Most larger series demonstrate associated neurologic
injury in fewer than 6% of patients, and it remains unclear if this is treatment- or injury-
instigated.34-36 Overall, the rate of open proximal ulna fractures (6%) is rare despite the
relative subcutaneous position of the fracture site.1

Transolecranon Fracture-Dislocations and Monteggia Variants
A transolecranon fracture-dislocation is an important defined pattern typically observed
in patients with good bone quality after a higher energy direct blow to the dorsal
forearm.37-39 The injury pattern typically results in a comminuted olecranon fracture
with the distal ulnar shaft and radius translated anteriorly and the distal humerus
dislocated dorsally. Conversely, Monteggia variants involve dissociation or disruption of

the proximal radioulnar joint and corresponding instability of the radiocapitellar joint.40-
42 The distinction between these two variants is critical given the potential associated
injuries (coronoid injury, shaft extension, and ligament disruption) that portend
substantial residual instability after simple fixation of the olecranon fracture alone.38
Patients with a transolecranon fracture-dislocations have displacement of the ulnar and
radial shafts in the same direction (implying no proximal radioulnar joint injury), whereas
in patients with a Monteggia variant, the ulnar and radial shafts displace in opposite
directions. These two injuries are frequently confused, and most current classification
systems describe only fracture pattern, location, and morphology, thereby providing
limited guidance on the treatment differences between these injuries.8,43
Injury Classification
The most common classification is the Mayo classification system.
Diverse number of alternative classifications
Additional subclassifications, including the Jupiter modification of the Bado proximal ulna
fracture-dislocation, incorporate olecranon fracture patterns.

Injury Classification
Of the existing classification systems, the Mayo classification system is the most practical
and clinically useful classification system and, therefore, is most frequently used44
(Figure 1). The Mayo classification, which is based on radiographs alone, uses fracture
type and elbow stability to distinguish fracture patterns and provides a treatment
algorithm based on fracture type.45 Fractures are stratified into nondisplaced fractures
(type I), displaced fractures with a stable ulnohumeral joint (type II), and displaced
fractures with presumed injuries to the collateral ligaments (medial and/or lateral
collateral ligament) and an unstable ulnohumeral joint (type III). Further
subcategorization describes the degree of comminution of each type: noncomminuted
(A) and comminuted (B).44 Most fractures are Mayo type II (80% to 85%), whereas a
smaller proportion represent true nondisplaced type I fractures (5% to 12%).46

The Bado classification system specifically addresses Monteggia fracture-dislocations of
the proximal ulna.42 In discussing olecranon fracture patterns, surgeons must be able to
identify Bado type IIA injuries, which is a subtype of the Monteggia variant classified by
Jupiter et al.51 This fracture pattern includes an olecranon fracture with extension to the
coronoid process and associated posterior radial head dislocation. This pattern requires
special attention to ensure careful anatomic re-creation of proximal ulna anatomy,
stabilization of the coronoid fragment, and relocation of the radial head.
The AO, Colton, and Schatzker classification systems also can be used to describe
olecranon fractures.52,53 The AO classification system is largely used for research
purposes. The Schatzker classification system groups fractures based on fracture
morphology, joint surface comminution, and associated injuries.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination
Initial evaluation of elbow trauma begins with a thorough patient history and physical
examination.
Physical examination should assess the patient completely. Patients affected by lower energy
trauma may require a more focused physical examination; however, for those affected by
high-energy trauma, Advanced Trauma Life Support protocols should be included in the
evaluation.

Patient History and Physical Examination
The patient history and physical examination should be carried out thoughtfully and
documented accurately with consideration of potential associated injuries. This prevents
overlooking potential associated injuries that may be critical to appropriate diagnosis
and management. A focused patient history should capture the mechanism of injury, the
level of energy of the trauma, previous elbow pathology, symptom severity, and any
associated injuries. Physical examination should focus on assessment of skin integrity
and the presence of proximal or distal joint involvement or pain. Given its subcutaneous

location, olecranon fractures occasionally can be palpated directly. Documentation of
neurovascular function also is paramount.
Imaging Studies
Standard radiographs in the AP, lateral, and oblique planes are used for primary assessment.
Careful evaluation for associated bony injury or joint instability is key.
CT may be useful in specific patients with more complex fracture patterns to understand
associated injury patterns and fragment positioning.54

Imaging Studies
Evaluation of plain radiographs typically is adequate for assessment of the fracture
pattern and the presence of associated elbow injuries. True lateral images are
particularly important to help document fracture extension, fracture pattern, and elbow
instability. The ulnohumeral and radiocapitellar joints should be carefully inspected to
diagnose instability or associated injuries that may affect management. Although rarely
necessary for most fracture patterns, CT may afford additional insight into fracture
extension about the coronoid and radial head if these patterns are suspected. von
Rüden et al54 highlighted the need for careful scrutiny of radiographs, particularly
identification of the intermediate fragment, which is present at the center of the
trochlear groove and may require special attention. This articular free fragment may
block reduction or lead to malreduction, leading to early articular degenerative changes
if not adequately identified and managed. In their series, CT aid in identification and
preoperative planning for such cases.
Management
Management of olecranon fractures focuses on the maintenance/restoration of joint stability,
repair of the elbow extensor mechanism, restoration of the articular surface, and prevention
of complications, including stiffness.
Treatment options include

Nonsurgical management
Tension-band wiring (TBW),
Intramedullary screw fixation
Plate osteosynthesis
Fragment excision and triceps advancement
Nonsurgical management was historically reserved for truly nondisplaced type I fractures.
Growing evidence currently supports that nonsurgical treatment may play an expanded role in
the elderly population.
Surgical treatment is indicated for active, healthy patients with joint instability, fractures with
disrupted articular congruency, and patients with a disrupted triceps extensor mechanism.
Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management is recommended for nondisplaced olecranon fractures in compliant
patients.
Management involves immobilization for 3 to 4 weeks followed by range of motion (ROM).55
Elderly patients with congruent ulnohumeral alignment, regardless of fracture displacement,
may be treated nonsurgically.
Indications
Mayo type I fractures without displacement (<2 mm)5
Intact extensor mechanism
Elderly, low-demand patient (age >65 years) with congruent but displaced olecranon fracture
in the absence of associated fractures

Indications
Nonsurgical management, first described by Perkins,56 has traditionally been reserved
for truly nondisplaced fractures of the olecranon. Historically, a maximum of 2 mm is
considered appropriate for nonsurgical management. Nondisplaced fractures should
remain nondisplaced with an intact extensor mechanism if the elbow is held in flexion to
90o.57 Management begins with immobilization in a position of comfort, typically
between 45o to 90o of flexion for 1 to 4 weeks for early partial consolidation. Variations of

immobilization have been reported, including splint, cast, and collar-and-cuff
immobilization. Mobilization within a safe arc is allowed after immobilization and
continued until radiographic fracture union.58-61 Strength and resistance training can
begin after radiographic union, typically after 8 to 10 weeks. Early mobilization is a
careful but critical step given the risk of displacement versus the risk of stiffness.
Although rarely performed in the younger, healthy population, support is growing for the
nonsurgical treatment of elderly patients because of the reported high rates of
complications associated with surgical treatment in this group.62,63 Despite variations in
nonsurgical treatment protocols in studies evaluating the outcomes of nonsurgical
management, indications for nonsurgical management are largely standardized.
Nonsurgical treatment is indicated in patients older than 65 years, low-demand patients,
and patients with multiple comorbidities who have a Mayo type II olecranon fracture that
is displaced more than 2 mm, a congruent elbow, and no associated fractures.64 The
absence of subluxation/dislocation is critical for a successful outcome and, therefore,
must be assessed carefully.59,61
Contraindications
Surgical treatment is recommended for patients with a fracture associated with instability of
the elbow and patients with associated fractures of the proximal ulna/humerus/radius.
Younger patients with displaced fractures

Contraindications
Important contraindications to nonsurgical management include unstable fracture
patterns, fracture-dislocations, displaced fractures (>2 mm) in healthy active patients,
and patients in whom nonsurgical treatment fails. In addition, patients who require early
mobilization of the extremities, such as polytrauma patients, typically are better treated
surgically.

Techniques/Procedures
Nonsurgical management requires early supportive immobilization, splint/cast or collar-and-
cuff, followed by early mobilization.
Outcomes
Outcomes of most elderly patients who are appropriately treated appear to be good to
excellent.
These outcomes are independent of displacement.

Outcomes
A paucity of prospective literature is available to guide the nonsurgical management of
olecranon fractures. In younger, healthy patients, nonsurgical treatment may have a
role; however, the available literature is limited. Putnam et al65 reported results from a
small pilot study that included 14 patients across a broad range of ages with a Mayo type
II olecranon fracture who were treated nonsurgically. The author reported good to
excellent functional results.
Interest of outcomes of the nonsurgical management of olecranon fractures in low-
demand elderly patients has substantially increased. A number of studies have reported
on the outcomes of nonsurgical treatment in the elderly patient population.59-61,64,66-68
These studies demonstrate a high frequency of nonunion in patients treated
nonsurgically (86%); however, overall functional scores and patient satisfaction were
excellent. In a meta-analysis, Chen et al66 reported a mean Disabilities of the Arm,
Shoulder and Hand score of 12.3 and a mean Mayo Elbow Performance Index score of
95.1. Overall patient satisfaction at a mean follow-up of 6 years from fracture was 91%,
suggesting that patients who underwent this treatment strategy were happy with their
outcome despite their radiographic findings. However, 17% of patients had limitations in
triceps strength, with an inability to push up from a chair.59 Although growing evidence
supports good to excellent outcomes in elderly low-demand patients, additional well-
constructed studies are necessary to fully elucidate the role of nonsurgical treatment.

Surgical Management
The goal of the surgical management of olecranon fractures focuses on the restoration of joint
congruency, stability, and repair of the extensor mechanism.
Numerous techniques are described to establish a stable and pain-free elbow.
The success of various treatment modalities depends on fracture morphology and a careful
understanding of the tools available for fixation.
TBW historically has been the preferred treatment modality for fixation of simple type II
fractures.
Plate fixation is commonly used for comminuted Mayo type II and type III fractures.
Newer techniques, including ulnar intramedullary fixation devices, have shown promising
results in limited series.
Indications
Surgical management is indicated for displaced, comminuted, unstable olecranon fractures.
Surgical management also is recommended for active patients with a minimally displaced
fracture to allow for early ROM of the elbow.

Indications
Surgical management is indicated for all unstable fractures in which the ulnohumeral
joint is subluxated and for fractures at risk of displacement in high-demand, young
patients. Typically, displacement of more than 2 mm is considered excessive. This
includes most olecranon fractures.1 Regardless of the selected treatment, the goals of
surgical management are anatomic reduction of the articular surface, restoration of
elbow congruence and bony alignment, and stable fixation to allow for early ROM.
Contraindications
Absolute contraindications to surgical management include active infection and medical
conditions that preclude surgical management.
Relative contraindications to surgical management include persistently unstable polytrauma
patients, patients with active substance abuse or psychiatric conditions, and patients with a

Contraindications
Although many olecranon fractures require surgical stabilization, several important
contraindications require delayed surgery management or may preclude surgical
management. For example, a physiologically unstable polytrauma patient who initially
may require a damage-control approach for the management of injuries. Patients with
poor or damaged soft tissue about the elbow also require careful consideration because
such injuries may limit fixation coverage These patients may require advanced closure
techniques or consultation with a plastic surgeon for flap coverage.
Techniques/Procedures
Multiple surgical constructs are available for fixation (TBW, plate fixation, intramedullary
fixation).
Fixation choice should be based on fracture pattern and the presence of instability.

Techniques/Procedures
Patient factors, fracture patterns, the presence of concomitant instability, the presence
of associated injuries, and surgical skill set are important factors to consider during
surgical planning. Reinforcing and revisiting surgical goals will help avoid pitfalls. Similar
to all surgical planning, a stepwise approach will mitigate errors (Video 1).

Patient Positioning
Patient positioning (supine, lateral, prone) is fracture and surgeon dependent.
Choice of surgical table is based on surgeon discretion. The author prefers a standard surgical
table for its ubiquity and simplicity.

Patient Positioning
Patient positioning includes supine, lateral and prone positions. Positioning typically is
determined based on a patient’s condition, associated injuries, and the surgeon
preference.
In the supine position, the patient’s arm is placed across the chest over a Mayo stand or
on blankets to bring the olecranon and elbow directly into the surgeon’s view. This
position is advantageous because of its simplicity and because it avoids manipulation of

polytrauma patients who may have associated injuries or spinal precautions. However,
the arm must be supported or held by a surgical team member and the elbow is flexed,
which generates a distraction force at the fracture site.
In the lateral decubitus position, the patient is supported by bolsters or a bean-bag
support, and the affected arm lies over an arm support with the forearm facing
downward. In this position, bony prominences must be carefully padded to prevent
pressure sores and neuropraxia. Advantages of this position include familiarity (similar
to distal humerus), freedom of the arm for manipulation, and ease of addressing
additional injuries; however, arm flexion places distraction forces through the fracture,
and the arm must be supported on a Mayo stand or supported by a surgical team
member for reduction. In addition, this position requires substantial repositioning, which
may be less than ideal for polytrauma patients.
The prone position is associated with several advantages, including the ease at which the
arm is positioned and access to the remainder of the humerus and forearm. This
position require additional care and time for appropriate setup and may not be an
option in polytrauma patients.
Surgical Approaches
The surgical approach to the olecranon, regardless of fixation strategy, involves a posterior
longitudinal incision directly over the olecranon tip or a gently curving medial or lateral incision
over the olecranon.30 The incision starts just proximal to the tip to allow for complete
exposure of the olecranon and extends distally over the dorsal olecranon surface, far enough
for metalwork insertion. Full-thickness flaps are raised to preserve vascularity to the skin.
Then, the dorsal surface of the olecranon typically is encountered. Minimal elevation of the
flexor carpi ulnaris/extensor carpi ulnaris subperiosteally helps expose the fracture for
reduction while preserving bony blood supply. Identification of the ulnar nerve usually is not
required.
Surgical Fracture Fixation
TBW technique over two Kirschner wires (K-wires or screws)

Indications: Isolated, transverse fractures that are proximal to the coronoid without
substantial comminution and not associated with ligamentous instability
This technique does not resist angular forces or stabilize complex fracture patterns.
Contraindications: Substantially comminuted fractures of the proximal ulna, especially those
with associated elbow instability
Insertion of K-wires into the anterior cortex of the ulna, distal to the fracture line, enhances
fixation strength and may help prevent backout. The surgeon must be aware of
overpenetration of the anterior cortex, which may result in decreased ROM because of
impingement on the proximal radius and an increased risk of injury to the anterior
interosseous nerve.
Plate fixation to the dorsal aspect of the proximal ulna
Dorsal plate application is the preferred fixation method in patients with comminution or
associated ligamentous injury with instability.
The terminal aspect of the triceps insertion can be split and then repaired after plate
application to minimize prominence.
Fragment excision and triceps advancement for osteoporotic, comminuted fragments
composing less than 50% of the olecranon
May be beneficial in elderly (>70 years), low-demand patients whose bones are osteoporotic
enough to compromise fixation (however, nonsurgical treatment of such patients currently
should be considered a superior option).

Surgical Fracture Fixation
Optimizing fracture fixation requires a careful understanding of the fracture pattern.
One reproducible and easy distinction that helps determine the appropriate fixation
strategy is the stability pattern of the fracture. Stable fractures are defined as transverse
fractures localized to the middle or proximal aspect of the trochlear groove without the
presence of comminution or subluxation. In these fractures, all techniques may be used,
including TBW, plate fixation, or intramedullary fixation. Traditionally, TBW has been
favored for the management of stable fracture patterns.
The TBW technique is achieved by inserting two parallel K-wires (1.6 or 2 mm) antegrade

Alternatives to this traditional technique include the use of cancellous screws rather

TBW technique involves the biomechanical principle of conversion of distraction forces
at the dorsal cortical surface into compression forces at the articular surface (Figure 3).
Although the main advantages of the technique are its simple premise, low profile, low
cost, and mechanical dynamic compression, studies have refuted many of these claims,
demonstrating that TBW techniques are extremely technique dependent, are associated
with high rates of metalwork prominence, and may not provide dynamic compression as
suggested. Schneider et al73 demonstrated the challenges of this technique, reporting
more than four technical imperfections per case in more than 2,300 procedures. Specific
technical pearls include bicortical fixation, which reduces pin migration; parallel wire
placement; and the use of two wire knots.74-76 The known risks of anterior cortical
perforation, such as neurovascular injury, can be minimized with less than 1cm
perforation anterior to the cortex at least 1.5 cm distal to the coronoid.75,77 Prominent
wires after TBW remain an issue, with rates as high as 65% to 80%.63,78,79 Finally, a
number of biomechanical studies have shown that compression at the articular surface
with TBW may not be as robust as that obtained with plate or compression-screw
fixation.6,80-83 Alternatively, intramedullary nailing also has been used for the
management of stable fractures.84-86 In theory, intramedullary nailing offers the
advantages of a low-profile, soft-tissue–friendly technique with the mechanical
advantages of intramedullary fixation mechanics.86 Although prospective, comparative
studies to support the use intramedullary nailing are lacking, small series and
biomechanical models suggest intramedullary nailing may have a role in olecranon

Intramedullary screw fixation of the olecranon was first described by
Macausland.88,89,90Traditionally reserved for more stable, transverse patterns, the
technique allows for compression and interdigitation at the fracture. In addition, data
have been reported regarding the use of an intramedullary screw for fixation of
olecranon osteotomies after distal humerus fixation.91,92 The steps are straightforward
and reproducible: After the fracture has been reduced, the intramedullary canal is
drilled. A posterior and central starting point on the olecranon is selected in line with the
canal. A screw of sufficient length is selected to ensure engagement of the partially-
threaded 6.5- or 7.3-mm screw with the endosteal diaphyseal bone. Care is taken to
appreciate the ulnar anatomy to avoid malreduction induced by deflection from the
ulnar bow. Care should be exercised with the 7.3-mm screw, which has less capacity for
bending and may result in malreduction. The canal is then tapped to prepare for
insertion of the cancellous screw. Typically, a screw longer than 120 mm (32-mm thread)
is selected to ensure adequacy of intramedullary endosteal thread engagement.93
Advantages of this technique include its low profile, rigid fixation and the ability to
generate articular compression directly and via a tension-band–like mechanism.89,90,94
Biomechanical studies have demonstrated the importance of diaphyseal engagement of
the screw for optimal fixation.95-97 A 6.5-mm screw typically provides ample cortical
purchase. Two additional aspects of the screw fit generate additional fixation, including
engagement of the screw with the cortical surface as a result of the varus proximal ulna
bow and the screw head against the cortical olecranon bone. Often, a washer can be
used to provide additional surface compression, particularly in osteoporotic bone.
Therefore, the importance of screw size, including length and diameter, screw starting
point, and trajectory, are technically critical for success and to avoid malreduction.91,98
Biomechanical studies have not demonstrated an advantage of screw fixation over plate
fixation in the management of transverse olecranon fractures.83,99,100 No direct, head-
to-head clinical comparisons between screw fixation and other techniques exist;
however, variable reports of metalwork irritation have been reported and appear to be
lower or equivalent to modern plating techniques.91,92,101 Screw fixation appears to
offer a low-profile, simple (albeit technically demanding) method of fixation for
transverse olecranon fractures and osteotomies, resulting in a lower complication rate
than traditional TBW.

Plate fixation was traditionally reserved for displaced fracture patterns with
comminution and fractures with concomitant instability. In addition, fractures extending
beyond the midpoint of the trochlear groove are appropriate for plate fixation. Plate
fixation can be performed with the use of one of many available constructs currently on
the market; however, pre-contoured plates with various configurations of locking screws
have gained popularity because of ease of application and possibly lower removal rates.
Despite this increased use, no biomechanical studies have demonstrated their
superiority.63,78,79,83,102,103 Although these plates fit a normal distribution of patients,
an understand an individual patient’s proximal ulna osteology is critical to avoid
malunion and mechanical malalignment of the joint.16 For example, applying a straight,
stiff plate to the dorsal ulna without considering a patient’s bone structure may induce
deformity by rotating and malreducing the dorsal 5.7o of angulation. In patients with a
comminuted fracture, reduction of the articular fragments under direct visualization
before reduction of the dorsal cortical fragments is necessary to restore articular
congruency. Beginning at the articular surface, using the trochlea as a template, the
articular fragments are reconstructed and temporarily stabilized. Moving dorsally, the
final dorsal cortical fragment can be placed, and definitive fixation can be applied. The
greater sigmoid notch should be re-created anatomically such that the radius of
curvature is not altered, which may lead to joint incongruity or subluxation and early
failure. The use of locking fixed-angle plates may be advantageous in patients with a
comminuted fracture, avoiding overcompression.7
Despite design modifications and optimization, the proximal segments of the olecranon
may be challenging to capture, and good fixation is difficult to achieve. In patients with
extensive comminution, osteopenia/osteoporotic bone, or small fragments, additional
support can be achieved via suture fixation. Edwards et al104 demonstrated the
importance of and the potential need for augmentation after plate fixation in osteopenic
bone, regardless of specialized implant designs. Biomechanically, the authors
demonstrated that early weight-bearing exercises well below the physiologic loading
forces required for even simple movements, such as pushing up from a chair, resulted in
catastrophic failure in all plate designs. Wild et al105 reported that suture fixation
through the triceps that is secured to the plate provides substantial additional stability to
the proximal olecranon fragments106 (Figure 5).

Postoperative Management
The goal of postoperative management is early mobilization to prevent complications
associated with prolonged immobilization.
Complications
Nonunion
Nonunion is rare; however, malunion, especially of unreduced, impacted articular fragments,
may result in posttraumatic arthritic changes and stiffness.
Malunion
Fracture malreduction/malalignment may lead to posttraumatic arthritis.
Careful consideration of olecranon morphology and patient-specific PUDA may help avoid
malalignment and additional consequences of malunion.
In complex cases (transolecranon and Monteggia fracture-dislocations) malunion may lead to
secondary elbow instability and catastrophic degenerative changes.
Hardware Failure/Loss of Reduction
Loss of reduction is rare if the proper principles of fixation are followed. TBW of fractures
associated with comminution or elbow instability may lead to failure of the construct and loss
of reduction and should be managed via plate fixation (Figure 6).

In most series, the most common complication after olecranon fracture is postinjury
stiffness. Terminal extension of 10o to 20o may be lost. Some studies report
improvement with removal of metalwork and concomitant release. However, overall,
functional ROM is the expectation after management. Nonunion is relatively rare after
surgically management, with rates lower than 1% to 4% reported across multiple studies
using various techniques.4,59,62,87,110,111 Symptom-free nonunions or fibrous unions are
frequently encountered after the nonsurgical management of displaced fractures in low-
demand, elderly patients. Despite their high frequency and apparent displacement,
these nonunions do not appear to affect function or patient outcomes.29,58,59 However,
malunion of the proximal ulna or the sigmoid notch articular surface may lead to
functional loss, including decreased ROM, functional blocks to motion, incongruence of
the ulnohumeral or radiocapitellar joints, and early posttraumatic changes at the
elbow.13,15,18 Fracture malreduction of more than 2 mm, specifically that affecting the
articular segments, may lead to midterm to long-term posttraumatic arthritis in as many
as 20% of patients.30 Narrowing of the trochlear groove as a result of extensive over-
compression or malreduction in patients with a severely comminuted fracture also is
associated with the development of postinjury arthrosis.45
Although serious complications are rare, patients should be informed about
symptomatic metalwork, which is the most common cause for revision surgery. Given
the subcutaneous nature of the olecranon, soft-tissue coverage is limited. Rates of
symptomatic metalwork are as high as 75% in some series on TBW fixation and may
exceed 50% in patients who undergo plate fixation.63,107,112,113 Newer, lower profile
plates may decrease the risk of symptomatic metalwork compared with historical
values.43 Overall, plate fixation may result in lower rates of irritation and prominence
than TBW fixation, whereas intramedullary nail fixation and suture constructs may result
in even fewer complaints of fixation prominence.102,114-116 In a randomized controlled
rial, Duckworth et al111 reported a lower overall complication rate with plate fixation
compared with TBW, which was particularly focused on a substantially lower rate of
metalwork removal (63% versus 38%). However, serious complications, such as deep
infection and revision surgery, occurred exclusively in the plating group. TBW fixation
also is associated with a higher rate of malunion and loss of reduction, with rates as high
as 50% compared with plate fixation.4,76,87,111 Infection rates remain low across series
(1% to 6%); similarly, low rates of nonunion also have been reported.62,63,78,85,111

Rehabilitation
Nonsurgically managed fractures that are minimally displaced with an intact extensor
mechanism may be splinted/casted or immobilized in a collar-and-cuff for 1 to 4 weeks.
Surgically managed fractures generally are splinted for as long as 1 week postoperatively for
pain control and to allow for swelling to subside.
Active and gentle passive motion is then initiated; however, resisted extension is specifically
restricted until clinical and radiographic evidence of fracture healing is observed, usually at 6
to 10 weeks postoperatively.
Older patients who rely on forceful elbow extension to push up from a chair or a toilet
should be advised to avoid this activity until complete fracture union occurs.

Rehabilitation
Overall, standardized, well-studied evidence is lacking with regard to the ideal
rehabilitation algorithm for patients with an olecranon fracture. The timing and degree
of early motion should be based on the status of the soft tissue and fixation stability.
With nonsurgical management, immobilization has been successfully achieved via cast
immobilization, splint immobilization, and collar-and-cuff options. This typically is
maintained for 1 to 4 weeks, with early active ROM initiated thereafter. Postoperatively,

posterior soft-tissue closure and unloads the triceps. An anterior slab typically is
preferred to avoid putting pressure on the wound. At 5 to 10 days, the slab generally is
removed, and an early ROM program initiated; however, a delay in strengthening

Outcomes
Good to excellent outcomes can be expected in most patients who undergo treatment
for the management of an olecranon fracture. Similar to other articular fractures, careful
articular reduction and restoration are correlated with longer term radiographic
success.6 Long-term outcomes from Sweden demonstrate that, overall, 96% of patients
had good or excellent results, with few patients reporting residual pain (4%).4 Nearly
one-half of the patients had degenerative radiographic findings, and severe arthrosis
occurred in 10% of the patients; however, limited correlation with functional outcomes
was reported.4,122 Globally, loss of motion, particularly terminal elbow extension, is a
common outcome after management. As many as 50% of patients may experience loss
of the terminal 10o to 15o of extension; however, this does not appear to affect
functional outcome scores.123
Despite various fixation techniques, little functional outcome data differentiates these
techniques if they are performed appropriately, likely reflecting the overall high degree
of satisfaction and union associated with olecranon fractures. Studies comparing TBW
and plate fixation for the management of olecranon fractures have reported no
substantial differences in Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand scores; Mayo Elbow
Performance Index scores; or ROM.4,87,111 Similar findings, albeit in fewer high-quality
studies, have been associated with intramedullary nail fixation.84,124 In addition, in the
elderly, low-demand patient population, successful patient-reported outcomes and

Pearls and Pitfalls
A careful assessment of the fracture pattern, concomitant injuries, and joint instability is
paramount to optimize successful selection of appropriate management.
Olecranon fractures are intra-articular injuries; therefore, anatomic reduction is preferred in
the medically-well patient.
Careful attention should be paid to the proximal ulna anatomy during reconstruction to
restore the PUDA, varus angulation, and greater sigmoid notch radius of curvature. The
tension-band technique should be used exclusively for fractures that are proximal to the base
of the coronoid and that occur secondary to eccentric loads.
Dorsal-contoured plate application is the preferred fixation method for fractures secondary to
bending mechanisms of injury (including those distal to the coronoid), fractures with
comminution, fracture-dislocations, and associated ligamentous injury with instability. The use
of pre-contoured plates may decrease hardware removal rates.
Patients should be informed that the risk of implant prominence and the need for later
hardware removal are common; however, overall outcomes are good.
